M11-01-READCEE.2:
You have the income statement as filed in the Italian statutory (CEE) format and two extracts from the notes to the accounts. There's no EBITDA line: build it yourself.

- EBITDA is operating profit **before** depreciation and impairments (B10) and provisions (B12): all the other B items are subtracted from the value of production, each with its sign (B11 can be negative).
- The notes reveal that B8 (use of third-party assets) contains {p0} of operating lease payments on core machinery. The listed peers apply IFRS 16 and don't have those payments in EBITDA: to compare them you need a management EBITDA that adds them back.
- Trade working capital uses receivables from customers **due within** 12 months; those due beyond are financing to the customer, not working capital.

M11-02-DIRTYTABLES.3: In {target} {cosa}, adding only the product rows with a conditional sum.
M11-02-DIRTYTABLES.7:
The target's CFO sends you the ERP extract by product. It looks clean, but it contains **subtotals by region** and the **grand total**: a SUM down the column counts every euro three times.

Add up only the detail rows: they all have a code starting with "PROD". Write the formulas so they stay right even if tomorrow the extract arrives with more rows: no cell-by-cell sums.
M11-02-DIRTYTABLES.title: Badly formatted tables: cleaning up and excluding spurious subtotals
M11-03-MIXEDUNITS.2:
Normalise budget data expressed in different units and currencies into **absolute Euros (€)**.

Raw input data:
- **Operating Revenue**: {p0} k€ (thousands of euros)
- **Operating Costs**: {p1} M€ (millions of euros)
- **Global Capex**: $ {p2} (in US Dollars)
- **EUR/USD Exchange Rate**: {p3} (dollars per 1 euro)

Each source uses its own unit: sales thinks in thousands, management control in millions, the American parent in dollars. Before adding them up they all need to be in euros. Watch the exchange rate: EUR/USD says how many dollars one euro is worth, so to go from dollars to euros you divide.

Convert the three items; net cash flow calculates itself.

M11-05-FINDERRORS.5:
The counterparty has sent you their model. The committee reads three numbers: **EBITDA**, **net income** and **free cash flow**. There are **three errors** in the model, and at least one of the three numbers is off.

Work out the order of magnitude in your head, then trace back the precedents of each result (F2 on a cell shows the formula) until you find the wrong cells. Fix them there, where they originate: rewriting the final result from scratch doesn't count as a fix.

Typical errors in a model you receive: numbers typed by hand where there should be a formula, ranges that skip a row, flipped signs, taxes calculated on the wrong base, constants hidden inside formulas instead of in the assumption cells.
M11-05-FINDERRORS.17: Start from costs: is the total really the sum of the three rows above, and is it a formula?
M11-05-FINDERRORS.18: Check the signs: EBIT deducts depreciation, free cash flow deducts capex.
M11-05-FINDERRORS.19: Taxes: IRES is calculated on profit before tax with the rate in B14, and the total includes IRAP.
M11-05-FINDERRORS.title: Finding planted errors: audit, hardcodes and inconsistent formulas

M11-06-RESTATEMENT.5:
Accounting due diligence has found two problems in the last two financial years: revenue recognised early and development costs capitalised that should have been expensed. They must be corrected retroactively.

- Equity at the start of year 1: {p0}; tax rate {p1}
- The adjustments are **pre-tax**: reducing pre-tax profit also reduces taxes, so net income falls only by the net part.
- Dividends already paid don't change: they really went out.

Compute restated earnings, restated equity at the end of year 2 and how much reported equity was overstated. Check: the overstatement is the sum of the net adjustments.
